headline: Tokyo courts Bishkek; Irad's antimony and orchards reach Japan on Kyrgyz paper
dek: Japanese trading houses buy Iradi antimony metal and trioxide, and Japanese glaciologists work with TSU, yet no Japanese office exists in the ISEZ and no ISEZ certificate carries weight in Tokyo.
paragraphs: Japan's ambassador to Kyrgyzstan said in an interview this week that Tokyo wants deeper economic ties with Bishkek. The remark concerned Kyrgyzstan alone. It nonetheless describes a buyer that Iradi exporters already sell to, through a neighbour's paperwork rather than their own.

Japan keeps no embassy or office in Irad. No state has an embassy in Talas; the foreign presences here are liaison offices and desks, and none carries Japan's flag. Yet Japanese trading houses buy Iradi antimony metal and trioxide, the products of the Sary-Bulak and Chatkal works, and Japanese glaciologists work with Talas State University at the Manas Peak observatory, where the retreat of the Talas Alatau's glaciers is measured.

The commercial side runs on borrowed documents. Antimony leaves the ISEZ on Kyrgyz certificates of origin, and orchard and farm goods go out on Kyrgyz or Kazakh veterinary and phytosanitary paper. An ISEZ certificate, however carefully stamped, counts for nothing outside the zone. As IradOne reported on Wednesday and again on Friday, the Talas investment forum earlier this month pitched rim orchards and antimony processing to foreign delegates, and Iradi buyers' links to Japan-sized markets run through the neighbours.

Prof. Raisa Akmatova, an economist at TSU, said the arrangement is less a hurdle for the buyer than for the seller. "A Japanese trader needs a paper his customs office will accept, and he gets it from Bishkek or Almaty," she said. "The exporter in Irad pays for that convenience, in fees and in a margin he does not control." She added that a buyer who wanted a direct supply contract would face a second question: who in Irad could be held to it in a court the buyer recognises.

The forum's own numbers show the scale of what is being sought. Its antimony pitch, the Restart Programme, promises about 420 permanent posts at Sary-Bulak and Chatkal, with a first stage costed at 168 million som, about US$20 million at the official rate of 8.40. The Investment Promotion Office counts 88 agreements worth US$2.4 billion signed since 2023 and says, as it has before, that signatures are not disbursements. No contract was signed at the forum.

Exporters pay in dollars at the bazaar rate, which the Bazar-i Kalan changers put at 11.95 som to sell this morning, while the state books its receipts at 8.40. Whatever margin Kyrgyz intermediaries take is therefore felt twice, once in the fee and once in the exchange gap. The Herald has not seen a published schedule of those fees. Kyrgyzstan collects them on all re-papered trade, which Iradi traders cite as one reason Bishkek is the most open of the three neighbours.

Asked whether the ISEZ has any channel to Tokyo comparable to a diplomatic mission, the External Relations Office, which handles the zone's dealings with neighbours, UNMI and Washington, had not replied by the time this edition went to press. It is not a foreign ministry, and the ISEZ keeps trade offices in Almaty, Bishkek, Istanbul, Dubai and Washington, but none in Tokyo.

The glaciologists are the one Japanese tie that needs no one's certificate. Their work with TSU rests on university arrangements and instruments, not export papers. For a would-be investor, the open question remains what a partner signs with when nobody in Irad can issue a document the world recognises. For now the answer is a Kyrgyz one, and Tokyo's courtship of Bishkek is likely to make it a more useful one.

iradone.headline: Japan Courts Bishkek for Investment; Irad's Buyers Reach It via Neighbours
